body:
First Eagle Investments is expanding its international wealth business to attract family office capital into specialist private credit strategies.

The US asset manager, overseeing $217bn in assets, is set to be acquired by US-listed investment firm Victory Capital. It has made hires in London and the Middle East and established a presence in Switzerland, extending its reach beyond its longstanding partnership with Amundi.

“What we were missing, I think, was a more targeted approach to the wealth sector,” says Rémi Casals, head of international wealth solutions, who joined First Eagle in May 2025.

The firm already serves 80 family offices worldwide, largely through “word of mouth”, but is now targeting large single-family offices directly, while continuing to reach smaller family offices and multi-family offices through private banks and wealth managers. “We do both, but we do both by design, not by accident.”

Larger single-family offices often prefer to deal directly with asset managers, he explains. This could create “a problem” for First Eagle if private banks have their own competing investment offerings, Casals acknowledges.

Amundi distributes three co-branded global equity and multi-asset funds, accounting for around $15bn in client assets and giving First Eagle access to markets including mainland China. “Amundi brings client relationship people, salespeople and client service on the ground, and we are the investment managers,” says Casals.

Alongside this arrangement, First Eagle has more than $1bn in international client assets through direct relationships outside the US. Its own distribution teams focus on strategies that Amundi does not distribute, particularly alternative credit, he says.

Family offices remain relatively lightly invested in private credit. Private debt accounted for 3 per cent of portfolios on average in 2025, compared with 17 per cent for private equity, according to UBS’s 2026 Global Family Office Report.

“Family offices have historically allocated heavily to private equity, but I think they are now looking to rebalance their portfolios towards private credit,” says Casals. “What may be slowing that rebalancing is growing concern about the refinancing cycle and emerging defaults in parts of the direct lending market.”

Not all family offices are reallocating capital from private equity to private credit, however.

“We are not seeing meaningful substitution from private equity to private credit,” says Richard Grimm, head of credit at Cambridge Associates, the global investment advisory firm serving institutional investors and wealthy families.

Instead, families are increasingly funding private credit investments from cash or public equities, he says, while expecting allocations to grow over the next three to five years, particularly in specialist strategies.

Preqin estimates the global private credit market at $2.3tn, while PitchBook forecasts it could reach $4.5tn by 2030.

First Eagle is concentrating on lower- and middle-market direct lending, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), asset-based lending and real-asset leasing, including railcars, through its alternative credit platform, Napier Park.

The firm has around $5bn invested in lower- and middle-market direct lending and approximately $30bn on its CLO platform. Smaller US borrowers can offer lenders tighter covenants and stronger protections than larger companies, which typically have greater bargaining power, Casals argues.

Private equity ownership is another feature of First Eagle’s lending strategy, with the firm favouring businesses backed by financial sponsors. “When a company is owned by private equity, if something is wrong, they will try to fix the company faster,” says Casals.

Cambridge Associates is also seeing growing interest in specialist private credit strategies, including asset-based lending and speciality finance, as investors seek to diversify their portfolios, Grimm says.

First Eagle’s more specialised private markets offering may appear a disadvantage alongside larger alternative asset managers with broader investment platforms. But being smaller can be an advantage in specialist credit, argues Casals.

“Sometimes for this asset class, not to be too big is better. When you’re too big, you start sometimes having to buy things you don’t want to buy,” he suggests.

Some family offices are satisfied with their allocations to larger alternative asset managers but increasingly see using specialist firms such as First Eagle as a way to diversify their portfolios beyond the industry’s dominant players, Casals says.

Beyond conventional corporate lending, First Eagle is pursuing strategies whose returns are driven by different factors from traditional bonds and direct lending.

Railcar leasing, for example, involves financing freight railcars used to transport goods across the US, generating income from contractual lease payments. Limited railcar supply and the relatively low cost of leasing compared with ownership give railcar owners pricing power, allowing them to maintain or increase lease rates, says Casals.

Credit quality has come under increasing pressure. The US private credit default rate reached 6.3 per cent in the 12 months to August 2026, its highest level in three years, according to loans monitored by Fitch Ratings.

The rapid growth of private credit has intensified competition, making manager selection increasingly important. “There is a lot of capital there. When more and more investors are going into the same space, that’s where you’re going to identify over time which asset managers are going to be able to be prudent and navigate these inflection points better than others,” says Casals.

Grimm at Cambridge Associates also warns that some borrowers took on “excessive leverage” during the low interest rate era, while the “deluge of retail capital” subsequently led to an oversupply of financing and “sub-par lending” in parts of the direct lending market.

“Together, that will result in some fund vintages of some fund managers underperforming what has otherwise been a resilient strategy that has generated consistent returns and consistent distributions,” says Grimm. “In general, this part of the market is more attractive to invest in today than it was in 2025; we are in the midst of some rationalisation that will make the opportunity more attractive.”

Higher borrowing costs remain a challenge, putting pressure on companies’ ability to service and refinance their debt. Elevated refinancing costs can trigger defaults, says Casals, expecting some borrowers to face further “stress” if interest rates remain high.

Highly leveraged software companies are one area of vulnerability, he says, warning that businesses which borrowed heavily during years of cheap financing could face additional pressure as AI threatens to disrupt parts of the industry.

By contrast, he sees opportunities in industrial businesses, as geopolitical tensions, tariffs and supply-chain disruptions encourage companies to bring manufacturing closer to home.

Liquidity pressures also persist, although redemption requests have begun to ease. Investors sought to withdraw $9.6bn from 13 non-traded private credit funds in the third quarter of 2026, equivalent to 10.1 per cent of their value, down from 11.2 per cent in the previous quarter, according to data from US research firm Robert A. Stanger & Co.

Against this background, transparency about investment risks and ensuring that investors’ access to their money is “aligned with the liquidity” of the underlying assets are essential, says Casals.

“If they have a pick-up in yield, they sometimes understand that they have to lock the capital for one year or two years. And if they want something more liquid, then they know that the yield they can get would be reduced.”

Investor education is also part of First Eagle’s efforts to win new family office business. Casals describes a recent meeting in Zurich with a prospective family office client considering its first CLO investment, for which the firm is arranging sessions with its investment teams in Zurich and London.

First Eagle’s international expansion comes amid a change in ownership. Founded as a family-owned business in 1864, First Eagle remained partly family-owned until 2025, when the family’s remaining stake was sold to private equity firm Genstar Capital. The asset manager is now set to be acquired by Victory Capital in a deal expected to close by the end of the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and client consent.

The deal, which would create a combined business managing $570bn, is an opportunity to support First Eagle’s longer-term growth, says Casals. The two firms have “complementary” investment capabilities, with First Eagle specialising in multi-asset strategies, global equities and alternative credit, while Victory Capital is more focused on US equities and fixed income.

Ownership by another asset manager offers greater stability than private equity ownership, he argues, describing the latter as having a more “financial approach” to ownership. “An asset manager is here to build much longer-term organisations and teams,” he says. Private credit will remain the focus of First Eagle’s international wealth business over the next three years, although its offering could broaden following the acquisition.

Despite its expansion plans, the firm is not setting specific fundraising targets for its family office business. “We don’t like to quote numbers,” Casals says, adding that the aim over the next three to five years is to serve more family offices in the UK, Switzerland and the Middle East. “For us, it’s more like the quality of the relationship we will establish.”

The firm’s long-term relationships with family offices also allow it to remain a “patient asset allocator”, investing prudently, deploying capital only when opportunities arise, avoiding speculation and holding assets for the long term, says Casals.

“For me, the biggest luxury we have in the world is time. Our clients give us the luxury of time.”
